summary:
I built a web application that receives data from MODIS and VIIRS and harmonizes both into one format. The fire activity can then be shown on a world map — for the whole world or for a small area.

I think, that most of NASA' sites is really hard to understand so I tried to keep the app as simple as possible so that people can see what is going on without having to learn how the app works.

That matters because most sites show this data in a way that is harder to understand than it needs to be.
details:
What it does

I built a web app that turns two satellite fire records into one. You pick an area (draw a rectangle, type coordinates or search for a city) and a period. The app shows the hotspots on a map, a burning calendar by year, month and day, and how the selected month compares with the median of the same days in earlier years. Everything on screen can be downloaded as CSV.

How it works

MODIS (1 km, since 2001) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012) rate fires differently. I harmonize them: VIIRS low confidence is dropped, nominal becomes 50, high becomes 90; MODIS below 50 is dropped. Two detections in the same 1 km cell on the same day count once, and the record keeps whether MODIS, VIIRS or both saw it. The result is one series of 8.7 million detections from 2001 to 2026. Cells are H3 hexagons, so counts are comparable everywhere and the map draws about 17,700 shapes for a worldwide week instead of 291,000 points.

Benefits and impact

Fire agencies and land managers usually get another red dot on a map. This app answers a different question: is this month normal? A forest service sees whether the season starts earlier, scientists get one comparable series instead of two incompatible records, and civil protection gets a ratio against 25 years instead of a single snapshot.

Tools

Python with pandas, DuckDB and h3. FastAPI for the API. React 19, Vite and Leaflet for the frontend. Data: NASA FIRMS, MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS C2 NOAA-20.

What was creative

Treating the calendar, not the map, as the main view. Comparing a running month only with the same days of earlier years. And saying "no comparison" instead of inventing a number when the history does not cover the area.

What we considered

Comparability between the two sensors, honest gaps in the data, a color ramp that also works for color-blind users
